cultivar: Zhejiang population bushes (Jiukeng group) with Longjing 43 and other local cultivars in newer gardens
processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black: withered, rolled tightly, oxidised and dried, then sorted; the small Zhejiang leaf gives a slim, tight strand.
harvest_season: Spring (April) for the better lots; summer pickings were the bulk of the old export production.
appearance_dry: Slim, tight, straight dark strands with a glossy, almost grey-black lustre and few tips.
taste_profile: Clean and brisk with a moderate sweetness, light malt and a hint of dried fruit; a lean, bright black rather than a rich one.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at 90–95 °C, short steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes; takes a splash of milk.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest in small quantities, mostly within Zhejiang; drink within a year. Production is a fraction of what it was in the export decades and there is no vintage market.
description:
Yue Hong is Zhejiang's gongfu black, named after Yue, the ancient state whose heartland was Shaoxing, and made in the hill country around the city, with Zhuji its best-recorded home today and Shengzhou also named. Regular production dates from about 1950, when it served the drive to pay state debts in tea; it shrank again once that trade faded and green tea paid better. What survives is a small, decent regional black.

It is made in the standard gongfu way – withering, tight rolling, oxidation, drying, sorting – from the same small-leaf Zhejiang bushes that give Longjing and Mao Feng. The small leaf and tight roll give a slim, glossy strand and a lean, brisk cup, closer to a Keemun in weight than to the big-leaf southern blacks, but without Keemun's aroma.

In the cup it is clean and bright with moderate sweetness, light malt, a hint of dried fruit and a brisk finish; six short steeps in a gaiwan, or a three-minute pot that takes a splash of milk. It is not a tea to analyse so much as one to drink with breakfast.

It is sold as the current spring, mainly within Zhejiang, sometimes under a county name rather than the old brand; it rarely travels. Look for tight, even, glossy leaf and a fresh, sweet dry aroma; old stock goes flat quickly because there is little oil in the leaf to begin with.

It is worth a cup for the history, and as a reminder that the same Zhejiang bushes can go either way: pick a local black and a local green from the same spring and brew them side by side.
sources_note: The 1950s development for Soviet export and the Shengzhou production centre follow Chinese tea-history sources; current production figures are not documented.
history:
Yue Hong is thinly documented. The name points to Yue, the old state around Shaoxing, and regular production under this name is dated to about 1950. In the early years of the People's Republic it was one of the teas used to pay down state debts, which earned it the nickname 'patriotic tea'.

Accounts of its earlier roots differ. One runs the craft back to the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, another traces it through Yongyi, a tea business founded in 1917. Zhuji is its best-recorded home today, with a Yue Hong museum at Dongbaihu that opened in November 2017. Little is documented on how much is made now.
